study.title: Zechariah 11 The good and the useless shepherd, and the despised value of God's care
study.overview: The chapter brings together images of judgment, abandonment and rejection. In verses 1 to 3, the language of lament announces the fall of strong and prosperous regions, showing that what seemed stable can be consumed by divine judgment. In verses 4 to 14, the prophet acts as a shepherd in favor of a flock destined for death, but the people and their leaders despise this care, paying him an unreasonable wage and rejecting the covenant symbolized by the two rods, called Agrado and Union. In verses 15 to 17, God commands the prophet to represent a foolish shepherd, a figure of corrupt and oppressive leadership, whose final ruin is certain: the arm and the right eye are wounded, showing the loss of strength and discernment. Together, the chapter exposes both the responsibility of leaders and the gravity of rejecting God's care.

outline.title: I am sorry about the destruction of what seemed strong
outline.explanation: The opening summons to the weeping over Lebanon, the cypresses, the oaks of Bashan and the shepherds. The images of cedars, woods and young lions represent strength, glory and security, but all this is slaughtered. The text prepares the reader for a judgment that reaches seemingly invincible structures.

outline.title: The rejected pastor and the despised salary
outline.explanation: God commands the prophet to feed the flock destined for slaughter, but the buyers and shepherds exploit the sheep. The prophet assumes the function of pastor, breaks symbolic relations through the two rods and receives thirty coins of silver as payment a humiliating value. As he throws the payment to the potter and break the second rod, he shows the breaking of the covenant and brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

outline.title: The foolish shepherd and his final judgment
outline.explanation: The prophet must assume the instruments of a foolish shepherd to represent a ruler who does not care for the lost, does not seek the little ones, does not treat the wounds and still devour the flock. The final oracle utters disgrace against this useless shepherd, reaching his right arm and eye, images of power and discernment destroyed.

study.context: The notes link the chapter to the theme of the judgment on Jerusalem and the people in a state of infidelity, although there is a difference between commentators on the exact historical form of this judgment. Tyndale points out that the lament on Lebanon and Bashan introduces the section on good and bad shepherds and that the sheep represent the Hebrew people being handed over to the exploitation. Matthew Henry reads the chapter as a denunciation of the abandonment of the people who reject the Messiah, while Adam Clarke understands the beginning of the chapter as a reference to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish order, with possible initial application to the Chaldeans. The biblical text, however, keeps the focus on the symbolic actions of the prophet and the spiritual responsibility of the leaders.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter shows that God is not indifferent to the corruption of his people or to the violence of his leaders. Pastoral care is measured not by titles, but by concrete action: seeking, healing, sustaining and protecting. When this function is betrayed, God himself allows the coexistence structure to break, and even the signs of unity are broken. The two rods, Agrado and União, suggest that the relationship of the people with God and the internal brotherhood depend on the covenant; when the people despise divine care, lose peace and cohesion. The salary of thirty silver coins expressed extreme contempt for the one who serves, and the quotation of his disposal shows the depreciated value given to the pastor's work. In the end, the useless pastor reveals that leadership without compassion becomes destructive and will be judged by God. In Christian reading, many see in this chapter an announcement that finds echo in the rejection of Christ; this is a possible theological interpretation, supported by the notes, but the text itself first denounces the infidelity of the people and their leaders.

scholarViews.insight: The lament over Lebanon and Bashan presents the fall of what seemed strong and prepares the section on good and bad shepherds; these symbols represent God's judgment on proud powers.
The wages of thirty silver coins are treated as an unreliable and negligible payment to the shepherd, illustrating how God's care was rejected and assessed with disdain.
The oracle against the useless pastor shows that his arm and his right eye symbolize power and discernment; the punishment destroys them and ends his selfish government.

questions: What attitudes of the leaders in Zechariah 11 show exploitation rather than true care for the flock?
What do the two rods, Agrado and Union, teach about covenant, communion and spiritual responsibility?
How does the value of thirty silver coins reveal human contempt for faithful service?
study.practice: This chapter calls to examine any leadership you exercise or follow: does it seek the fragile, heal the wounded and protects the little ones, or just feeds on the flock? It also invites you to assess whether we are treating God's care as something precious or as something worthless. In practice, this means serving with real compassion, refusing religious manipulation and honoring the unity of God's people through concrete actions of care, justice and fidelity.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided differ from the historical scope of the prophecy: some relate it above all to the destruction of Jerusalem and others to an initial application to the Babylonian invasion, with subsequent reading linked to the rejection of Christ. Since the request restricts the study to the chapter and the notes, it is not possible to affirm with certainty a single final historical identification for each symbol. In addition, the text uses poetic and symbolic language, so that some images admit more than one interpretive reading.
